questions.explanation: The cost is per request, so reduce the work per request and the number of requests per client. Hand-blocking cannot keep up; the handshakes complete, so SYN cookies do nothing; and the link is not the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a SYN flood without SYN cookies.

items.label: The half-open queue fills
The server stores half-open entries
Real clients’ SYNs are dropped
SYN-ACKs go to forged addresses and get no reply
Forged SYNs arrive

questions.explanation: Each forged SYN costs an entry until it times out, so the queue fills and real users are turned away.

questions.prompt: A 64-byte spoofed query triggers a 3,200-byte reply. Attackers send 1 Gbit/s of such queries. How many Gbit/s reach the victim?
assumptions: Every query is answered
Replies all go to the victim
questions.explanation: Design implication: 50 Gbit/s is more than most single sites can take in, so defence has to live upstream, not on the servers.

flashcards.back: Volumetric (fills links), protocol (exhausts state), application (expensive requests).
The server stores nothing for a SYN; it rebuilds state from the returning ACK.
Reply size ÷ request size; the victim gets attack rate × factor.

sources.title: RFC 4987: TCP SYN Flooding Attacks and Common Mitigations
RFC 2827 (BCP 38): Network Ingress Filtering
AWS: Best Practices for DDoS Resiliency

mechanism.title: Where each flood bites and where it is stopped
steps: Every service has a narrowest point: link capacity, a table of connection state, or the work per request. A denial-of-service attack aims at one of them. Distributed attacks use many sources, from botnets of compromised devices to reflection through innocent servers, so they cannot be stopped by blocking one sender.

A SYN flood targets the TCP handshake. For each SYN, a server normally allocates an entry, sends a SYN-ACK and waits, resending a few times. Forged SYNs never complete, so entries pile up until the queue is full and real SYNs are dropped. SYN cookies, described in RFC 4987, let the server skip the entry: it encodes the connection details and a secret-keyed hash into its initial sequence number, and rebuilds them when a valid ACK returns.

Reflection attacks forge the victim’s address as the source of small UDP queries to servers that answer with much larger replies: open DNS resolvers, time servers or misconfigured caches. The victim receives the replies from thousands of legitimate-looking servers. The amplification factor, reply size divided by request size, multiplies the attacker’s bandwidth, and spoofing is possible only where networks do not apply ingress filtering as BCP 38 recommends.

Volumetric attacks must be absorbed where capacity exceeds the flood. Anycast announces the service from many sites so the flood splits among them, and providers’ scrubbing centres drop attack traffic by protocol, port and pattern before forwarding clean traffic. The origin should accept traffic only from the edge, so attackers cannot bypass it by aiming straight at the origin’s address.

Application-layer floods look like real users and arrive over completed connections, so network filters cannot tell them apart. Defences work per request: cache expensive responses, rate-limit by client, account or key, require challenges for suspicious clients, and shed load before the database falls over. Autoscaling helps briefly but turns an attack into a large bill if no limit is set.

useWhen: Any public service, since a modest flood can fill a small site’s link.
Designing an origin behind a CDN, load balancer or scrubbing service.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on per-address blocking against forged or widely distributed sources.
Avoid unlimited autoscaling as the only defence against request floods.

rows: SYN cookies, larger queues, edge proxies
Caching, rate limits, challenges, load shedding

numbers.title: Can the uplink survive a reflection attack?
assumptions: 64-byte spoofed query, 3,200-byte reply
Attackers send 1 Gbit/s of queries
The site has a 10 Gbit/s uplink
steps: Amplification: 3,200 ÷ 64 = 50.
Arriving at the victim: 1 Gbit/s × 50 = 50 Gbit/s.
Uplink headroom: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 times over capacity.
Even with filters on the servers, 40 Gbit/s of the flood is dropped at random before reaching them, real traffic included.
numbers.result: The site cannot defend itself behind its own uplink; the attack must be absorbed upstream by an edge or scrubbing provider.

india.title: SYN flooding and ingress filtering in the RFCs, and AWS guidance
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 4987 surveys SYN flooding attacks and mitigations, including SYN caches and SYN cookies, and explains their trade-offs. RFC 2827, also known as BCP 38, asks network operators to drop packets whose source addresses could not have come from the customer network that sent them, which blocks spoofing and therefore reflection. The AWS whitepaper on DDoS resiliency recommends reducing the attack surface, absorbing volumetric attacks at edge locations and scaling to absorb application-layer floods while protecting the origin.

pitfalls.trap: “We’ll block the attacking IPs.”
pitfalls.say: “The sources are forged or innocent reflectors, so I’d filter by protocol and absorb upstream instead.”

pitfalls.trap: “Autoscaling handles DDoS.”
pitfalls.say: “It helps with request floods for a while, but a volumetric attack fills the link first, and unlimited scaling becomes a bill.”

takeaways: Volumetric floods fill links, protocol floods exhaust state, application floods exhaust work.
SYN cookies let a server keep no state until the handshake completes.
Amplification = reply size ÷ request size; spoofing makes reflection possible.
Absorb floods upstream and let the origin accept traffic only from the edge.

interactive.title: Attackers found your origin
interactive.prompt: Your site sits behind a CDN, but a flood now hits the origin servers’ public address directly, bypassing the CDN. What do you do first?

choices.label: Add more origin servers to absorb the traffic
choices.feedback: More servers behind the same link do not help once that link is full, and they cost money during the attack.

choices.label: Accept only the CDN’s address ranges, then move the origin
choices.feedback: Right: with the origin closed to everyone but the edge, direct floods are dropped upstream, and a new address the attackers do not know ends the bypass.

choices.label: Lower the DNS TTL on the site’s main record
choices.feedback: The attackers already have the origin’s address; DNS changes do not stop traffic aimed straight at it.

interactive.reveal: An origin behind an edge should accept traffic only from that edge, ideally through a private connection or firewall rules at the network level, and its address should not leak through old DNS records, mail headers or certificates. Then volumetric attacks land on the edge, which has the capacity to absorb them.

seeAlso.why: Rate limiting algorithms behind per-client limits for request floods
CDN edges absorb floods and hide the origin
Autoscaling helps briefly with request floods but needs limits

title: Nagle’s Algorithm and Delayed ACKs
objectives: Explain what Nagle’s algorithm and delayed ACKs each save
Diagnose the stall when a sender writes a request in two pieces
Choose between combining writes and disabling Nagle

cards.title: Two good ideas that collide
cards.body: Nagle’s algorithm (RFC 896) stops a sender from flooding the network with tiny packets: while any sent data is unacknowledged, small writes are held until an ACK arrives or a full segment builds up. A delayed ACK (RFC 1122) lets a receiver wait briefly, hoping to carry the ACK on its own reply; it must still ACK at least every second full-sized segment and within 500 ms. Each saves packets. Together they can deadlock briefly.

cards.title: Worked example: the 40 ms stall in write-write-read
cards.body: A client sends a request as a header write followed by a body write, then waits for the reply.
steps: The header (200 bytes) goes out at once, since nothing is unacknowledged
The body (300 bytes) is held by Nagle, because the header is not yet ACKed
The server cannot reply without the body, so it has nothing to carry an ACK and delays it
The delayed-ACK timer fires: 40 ms is a common Linux minimum, and some systems wait 200 ms
The ACK frees the body, the server replies, and the request finishes about 40 ms late
cards.note: Result. In a data centre with a 0.5 ms round trip, a call that should take about 1 ms takes about 41 ms, roughly 40 times slower, and the delay does not depend on payload size.

cards.title: Fix the write pattern first
cards.body: The cleanest fix is to send each message in one write: build the header and body in one buffer, or use a gather write that hands the kernel several buffers at once. Request and response protocols, such as most RPC and database clients, also set TCP_NODELAY to turn Nagle off, since they care about latency per message. With Nagle off, many tiny writes do become many tiny packets, so buffer in the application.

cards.title: Misconception: delayed ACKs are the bug
cards.body: Each feature helps on its own: delayed ACKs roughly halve ACK traffic on bulk transfers, and Nagle protects slow links from one-byte packets. The stall comes from the pattern, a sender that waits for an ACK the receiver will not send until it has more data. Remove the pattern with one write per message, or turn Nagle off for that socket; turning off delayed ACKs everywhere costs more and is not portable.

cards.title: Trap: benchmarks that only ever send one write
cards.body: A test that sends each request in a single write never sees the stall, so it passes, while production code with a separate header write is slow. The tell is latency stuck near 40 ms or 200 ms whatever the payload size, and in a packet capture, a gap of exactly that length before the second segment. Test with the real client library and the real message pattern.

questions.prompt: What does Nagle’s algorithm do?

choices.label: Delays ACKs so they can ride on replies
Splits large writes into MSS-sized segments
Holds small writes while sent data is unACKed
Resends lost segments sooner than the timer

questions.explanation: Nagle batches small writes on the sender. Delaying ACKs is the receiver-side feature; splitting into segments happens anyway; and early resends are fast retransmit, a different mechanism.

questions.prompt: Why does a receiver delay its ACKs?

choices.label: To send fewer ACKs, often carried on its reply
To slow down a sender that is too fast
To wait for the sender to send its FIN
To give the congestion window time to grow

questions.explanation: Combining the ACK with a reply saves packets. Slowing a sender is the receive window’s job; the FIN is unrelated; and the sender’s window grows on ACKs, so delaying them slows growth.

questions.prompt: Requests inside a data centre (0.5 ms round trip) take a flat 40 ms. The client writes the header and the body separately. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The server’s thread pool is too small
Nagle holds the body while the server delays its ACK
Each request sets up a new TLS session
The switches in the path add 40 ms of queueing delay

questions.explanation: A flat delay matching the delayed-ACK timer, with split writes, is the classic sign. A small thread pool gives delays that grow with load; a TLS setup costs round trips, about 1 ms here; and switch queueing is microseconds to a few ms.

questions.prompt: Which fix removes the stall without filling the network with tiny packets?

choices.label: Turn off delayed ACKs on every server
Set TCP_NODELAY and keep writing byte by byte
Increase the receive window on the server
Send the header and body in one write

questions.explanation: One write per message gives Nagle nothing to hold. Disabling delayed ACKs everywhere is costly and not portable; TCP_NODELAY with byte-sized writes sends a packet per byte; and the window is not the limit.

questions.prompt: Which workload actually benefits from Nagle’s algorithm?

choices.label: An RPC service exchanging small requests and replies
A multiplayer game sending a position update every 16 ms
A remote terminal over a slow link, one key per write
A database client sending short queries

questions.explanation: Batching keystrokes saves many 41-byte packets on a slow link. RPC calls, game updates and database queries are latency-sensitive messages that should go out at once, which is why their clients usually set TCP_NODELAY.

questions.prompt: Order the events in the write-write-read stall.

items.label: The server delays its ACK while waiting for the body
The client sends the header immediately
The body goes out and the server replies
Nagle holds the body until the header is ACKed
The delayed-ACK timer fires and the ACK is sent

questions.explanation: Each side waits for the other until the receiver’s timer breaks the tie.

questions.prompt: A 1-byte keystroke goes in its own IPv4 packet with a 20-byte IP header and a 20-byte TCP header. What percentage of the bytes is payload?
assumptions: No TCP options
Link-layer framing ignored
questions.explanation: Sanity check: about 98% of such a packet is header, which is the waste Nagle was designed to cut on slow links.

flashcards.back: Hold small writes while sent data is unacknowledged.
The receiver waits briefly to carry its ACK on a reply; at least every second full segment, under 500 ms.
One write per message, or TCP_NODELAY on latency-sensitive sockets.

sources.title: RFC 896: Congestion Control in IP/TCP Internetworks
RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts, section 4.2.3.2
man7: tcp(7)

mechanism.title: How two packet savers create a pause
steps: A TCP sender can send data as soon as the application writes it. On a slow, shared link in the 1980s, terminals sending one keystroke per packet spent about 40 bytes of headers on every byte typed. John Nagle’s rule, RFC 896, fixed that: if any data is in flight and unacknowledged, hold new small writes and send them together when the ACK arrives or a full segment is ready.

Receivers made a matching optimisation. Instead of acknowledging every segment at once, a receiver may wait a short time, because the application will often reply and the ACK can ride on that reply for free. RFC 1122 bounds the wait at 500 ms and requires an ACK for at least every second full-sized segment, so bulk transfers are acknowledged promptly.

The two collide when a sender writes a message in two parts and then waits for a reply. The first part goes out immediately. The second is small and data is unacknowledged, so Nagle holds it. The receiver has only part of the message, so it has no reply to send and delays its ACK. Neither side moves until the receiver’s delayed-ACK timer fires.

The timer length sets the penalty. Linux commonly uses a minimum of 40 ms, adjusting with observed round trips; other systems have used 200 ms. In a data centre with sub-millisecond round trips, the timer is many times longer than the request itself, so a service can be dozens of times slower than it should be with no sign of load.

There are two clean fixes. Write each message in a single call so there is never a held second part, which also saves system calls. Or set TCP_NODELAY on the socket so small writes go out at once, which most request and response libraries do; then the application should batch its own writes to avoid sending many tiny packets.

useWhen: Diagnosing latency stuck near 40 ms or 200 ms for small requests.
Choosing socket options for RPC, database or game protocols.
avoidWhen: Avoid turning off delayed ACKs system-wide as the fix.
Avoid TCP_NODELAY combined with many tiny writes per message.

rows: Nagle on, one write per message

numbers.title: The price of a split write
assumptions: Round-trip time 0.5 ms, server work 0.5 ms
Delayed-ACK timer 40 ms
Client writes header and body separately
steps: Expected latency with one write: 0.5 ms RTT + 0.5 ms work = 1 ms.
With a split write the body waits for the delayed ACK: + 40 ms.
Actual latency ≈ 41 ms, about 41 times the expected 1 ms.
A client doing 100 such calls one after another spends 4.1 s instead of 0.1 s.
numbers.result: A pattern bug, not load, multiplies latency forty-fold; one write per message removes it.

india.title: Nagle and delayed ACKs in the RFCs and the Linux manual
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 896, written by John Nagle in 1984, describes the small-packet problem and the rule of holding new data while earlier data is unacknowledged. RFC 1122 section 4.2.3.2 lets hosts delay ACKs, but requires an ACK for at least every second full-sized segment and a delay under 0.5 seconds. The Linux tcp(7) manual page documents TCP_NODELAY, which disables Nagle on a socket, and TCP_QUICKACK, which only temporarily leaves delayed-ACK mode.

pitfalls.trap: “The network adds 40 ms.”
pitfalls.say: “A flat 40 ms with split writes is Nagle meeting a delayed ACK; I’d send one write per message.”

pitfalls.trap: “Just disable delayed ACKs everywhere.”
pitfalls.say: “The pattern is the problem; one write per message or TCP_NODELAY on that socket fixes it without changing every host.”

takeaways: Nagle holds small writes while data is unacknowledged; delayed ACKs wait to ride on replies.
Write-write-read stalls until the delayed-ACK timer, often 40 ms or 200 ms.
Send each message in one write, or set TCP_NODELAY and buffer in the app.
Latency flat near the ACK timer regardless of size is the tell.

interactive.title: Guess the latency
interactive.prompt: A client in the same data centre as its server (0.5 ms round trip) sends each request as two writes, a header then a body, and waits for the reply. Nagle is on, and the server delays ACKs with a 40 ms timer. The server needs 0.5 ms per request. What latency do you expect?

choices.label: About 1 ms
choices.feedback: That is the latency with one write per message. Here the body waits for an ACK the server is holding back.

choices.label: About 41 ms
choices.feedback: Right: Nagle holds the body until the header is acknowledged, and the server holds the ACK until its 40 ms timer fires.

choices.label: About 80 ms
choices.feedback: The timer fires once per request: after it the body goes out and the reply follows within about a millisecond.

interactive.reveal: Each side waits on the other until the delayed-ACK timer breaks the tie, so the request costs the timer plus the normal 1 ms. Combine the writes or set TCP_NODELAY, and latency drops back to about 1 ms.

seeAlso.why: TCP acknowledgements and segments, which both features change
RPC frameworks that set TCP_NODELAY for low-latency calls
Why latency, not bandwidth, dominates small request and reply messages

title: VPNs and Tunnels: IPsec, WireGuard and Overlays
objectives: Explain how a tunnel wraps one packet inside another and what the outer header buys
Work out how much each tunnel header takes from the inner MTU
Choose between full and split tunnelling, and between site-to-site and per-user VPNs

cards.title: A packet inside a packet
cards.body: A tunnel takes a whole IP packet and carries it as the payload of another one. The outer header is addressed between the two tunnel endpoints, so the network in between only sees traffic between them; the inner header still names the real source and destination. IPsec in tunnel mode and WireGuard also encrypt and authenticate the inner packet, which is what makes them VPNs. GRE and VXLAN only encapsulate: they join networks without hiding anything.

cards.title: One packet through a site-to-site VPN
cards.body: The office router and the cloud gateway are the only machines that see the outer header.
steps: A laptop in the office sends a packet to 10.20.0.15, a server in the cloud network
The office router’s route table says 10.20.0.0/16 goes through the tunnel
The router encrypts the packet and wraps it in a new IP header addressed to the cloud gateway’s public address
The internet routes the outer packet like any other between two public addresses
The gateway checks the authentication tag, decrypts, strips the outer header and forwards the original packet

cards.title: Worked example: what each wrapper costs the MTU
cards.body: Every outer header comes out of the 1,500 bytes the physical link carries.
steps: WireGuard over IPv4: outer IP 20 + UDP 8 + WireGuard header 16 + authentication tag 16 = 60 bytes, leaving 1,440
WireGuard over IPv6: the outer IP header is 40 bytes, so 80 bytes of overhead and 1,420 left, which is why 1,420 is a common default
VXLAN carries a whole Ethernet frame: inner Ethernet header 14 + outer IP 20 + UDP 8 + VXLAN 8 = 50 bytes, so the inner IP MTU is 1,450 unless the underlay carries larger frames
IPsec ESP in tunnel mode: the overhead depends on the cipher and padding, commonly 50 to 80 bytes; check the vendor figure
TCP inside the tunnel: MSS = inner MTU − 40, so 1,400 for a 1,440-byte WireGuard tunnel over IPv4
cards.note: Result. A tunnel shrinks the largest packet by 50 to 80 bytes, so the interface MTU or the MSS has to shrink with it; otherwise large packets need fragmenting or vanish, as the layers lesson describes.

cards.title: Full tunnel or split tunnel
cards.body: A full tunnel sends all of a user’s traffic, internet included, through the VPN, so the company’s filters and logging see everything, at the price of hauling video calls and downloads through its gateway. A split tunnel sends only company prefixes through the VPN and the rest straight out, which saves gateway capacity and latency but leaves internet traffic outside company controls. Decide per prefix, and remember DNS: a split tunnel must still send internal names to the internal resolver.

cards.title: Trap: overlapping private address ranges
cards.body: Tunnels join networks that were numbered separately. If the office uses 10.0.0.0/16 and the cloud network also uses 10.0.0.0/16, the router cannot tell which side an address belongs to, and the tunnel comes up but traffic goes nowhere. Plan non-overlapping ranges before connecting networks; when that is too late, NAT on one side is a workaround that makes logs and allow-lists harder to read.

cards.title: Overlays: tunnels as the data-centre fabric
cards.body: Cloud and container networks often run an overlay: every host wraps its virtual machines’ packets in VXLAN or a similar header, addressed to the destination host. The physical network, the underlay, only routes between hosts, while each tenant gets its own virtual network with its own addresses. VXLAN’s 24-bit network identifier allows about 16.8 million segments, against 4,094 VLAN IDs on one Ethernet network.

questions.prompt: A packet crosses the internet inside a site-to-site tunnel. What does a router in the middle of the internet see?

choices.label: The laptop’s private address as the source
The two tunnel endpoints’ public addresses
The private server address, with the payload encrypted
The office router’s address and the server’s private address

questions.explanation: The outer header names only the tunnel endpoints. The laptop and server addresses are in the inner header, which a VPN encrypts; and no header mixes the router’s public address with a private destination, which the internet could not route.

questions.prompt: Which of these only encapsulates traffic and does not encrypt it?

choices.label: WireGuard
IPsec ESP in tunnel mode
VXLAN
A TLS-based remote-access VPN

questions.explanation: VXLAN wraps Ethernet frames in UDP to build overlay networks and has no encryption of its own. WireGuard, IPsec ESP and TLS-based VPNs all encrypt and authenticate the inner traffic.

questions.prompt: A WireGuard tunnel runs over IPv4 on a 1,500-byte path. What is the largest inner packet that fits without fragmenting the outer one?

choices.label: 1,500 bytes
1,460 bytes
1,440 bytes
1,420 bytes

questions.explanation: Outer IPv4 (20), UDP (8) and WireGuard (32) take 60 bytes, leaving 1,440. 1,500 ignores the wrapper; 1,460 is the ordinary TCP MSS with no tunnel; and 1,420 is what is left when the outer header is IPv6.

questions.prompt: A company wants staff video calls to stop crossing its VPN gateway while internal apps stay private. What should it configure?

choices.label: A split tunnel carrying only the company prefixes
A full tunnel with a larger gateway
A second VPN dedicated to video traffic
A VXLAN overlay from each laptop to the office

questions.explanation: A split tunnel routes company prefixes through the VPN and everything else directly. A full tunnel keeps hauling video through the gateway; a second VPN still sends it through company equipment; and VXLAN is for joining hosts in a fabric, not for remote users.

questions.prompt: A new tunnel between an office and a cloud network is up, but nothing gets through. Both sides number their hosts from 10.0.0.0/16. What is wrong?

choices.label: The tunnel is missing a certificate
The routers cannot tell which side owns an address
Private addresses are not allowed inside tunnels
The tunnel needs a larger MTU to carry 10.x traffic

questions.explanation: With the same range on both sides, the local route wins and tunnel traffic never leaves. A missing certificate stops the tunnel coming up at all; private addresses inside tunnels are the normal case; and MTU affects large packets, not every packet.

questions.prompt: Order what happens to a packet sent through a site-to-site VPN.

items.label: The router encrypts the packet and adds an outer header
The far gateway verifies, decrypts and forwards the inner packet
The host sends a packet to a private address in the other network
The internet routes the outer packet between the endpoints
The local router matches the route that points into the tunnel

questions.explanation: Route, wrap, cross the internet, unwrap. Only the two gateways ever see both headers.

questions.prompt: VXLAN identifies each virtual network with a 24-bit number. About how many million segments does that allow?
assumptions: All 2^24 values counted
Reserved values ignored
questions.explanation: Design implication: about 4,000 times the 4,094 usable VLAN IDs, which is why multi-tenant clouds build tenant networks as overlays rather than VLANs.

flashcards.back: A whole packet carried as the payload of another, addressed between the two endpoints.
60 bytes (IP 20, UDP 8, WireGuard 32), leaving 1,440 of 1,500.
Only company prefixes go through the VPN; the rest goes straight out.

sources.title: RFC 4301: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol
RFC 4303: IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)
RFC 7348: Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN)
AWS Site-to-Site VPN: customer gateway devices

mechanism.title: How a tunnel carries one network across another
steps: A tunnel has two endpoints, each with an address the network between them can route, usually a public address on the internet or a host address in a data centre. Each endpoint has a route table entry saying which inner destinations belong on the far side.

When a packet matches such a route, the endpoint adds a new outer header addressed to the other endpoint. Plain encapsulations such as GRE or VXLAN stop there. VPN protocols first encrypt the inner packet and add an authentication tag, so the network in between cannot read or alter it without detection.

The outer packet travels like any other. Routers and firewalls on the way see only the endpoints, a protocol number or a UDP port, and the outer size. Running over UDP, as WireGuard and VXLAN do, lets the tunnel cross NAT devices and spreads flows across equal-cost paths using the UDP source port.

The far endpoint checks the tag, decrypts, removes the outer header and forwards the original packet on its own network. Replies take the reverse route through the same pair, so both ends need routes for each other’s ranges, and those ranges must not overlap.

Every outer header consumes part of the link’s MTU, so the inner interface gets a smaller one. Endpoints either advertise the smaller MTU, clamp the TCP MSS in passing SYNs, or rely on path MTU discovery inside the tunnel. Site-to-site services commonly offer two tunnels to different gateways so maintenance on one does not cut the link.

useWhen: Joining an office or data centre to a cloud network over the internet.
Giving remote staff access to private applications.
Building per-tenant virtual networks on a shared physical fabric.
avoidWhen: Avoid a full tunnel when most traffic is internet video and the gateway is small.
Avoid connecting networks whose address ranges overlap without a plan.

rows: Site-to-site links between routers and cloud gateways
Remote access and simple site links
Carrying routing between sites, often inside IPsec
Overlay networks between hosts in a data centre

numbers.title: Sizing a remote-access gateway
assumptions: 1,000 staff on a full tunnel, each averaging 2 Mbit/s in working hours (illustrative)
Video calls are 70% of that traffic (illustrative)
Gateway capacity 1 Gbit/s
steps: Full tunnel load: 1,000 × 2 Mbit/s = 2,000 Mbit/s = 2 Gbit/s.
That is twice the 1 Gbit/s gateway, so calls and apps suffer together.
Split tunnel: video goes direct, so 30% stays: 0.3 × 2 Gbit/s = 0.6 Gbit/s.
Utilisation: 0.6 ÷ 1 = 60%, which leaves headroom for growth and for busy days.
numbers.result: Moving the 70% of traffic that is internet video off the tunnel cuts gateway load from 2 Gbit/s to 0.6 Gbit/s under these illustrative figures.

india.title: A branch office joined to a cloud network
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: A lending company in Pune runs its loan system in a cloud network numbered 10.20.0.0/16 and its branch offices in Nashik and Kolhapur on 192.168.10.0/24 and 192.168.20.0/24. Each branch router keeps two IPsec tunnels to two cloud gateways, with routes for 10.20.0.0/16 through both, so one gateway can be patched without cutting the branch off. Staff internet traffic leaves locally, so a branch’s 50 Mbit/s line is not spent on video calls through the cloud, and the tunnel interface MTU is lowered so loan documents uploaded from scanners do not stall.

pitfalls.trap: “The tunnel is up, so routing is fine.”
pitfalls.say: “An up tunnel only proves the endpoints agree; I’d check routes on both sides and that the address ranges do not overlap.”

pitfalls.trap: “Put everyone on a full tunnel for security.”
pitfalls.say: “A full tunnel adds inspection but hauls all internet traffic through the gateway; I’d size it or split company prefixes from the rest.”

takeaways: A tunnel carries a whole packet inside another, addressed between two endpoints.
VPNs encrypt the inner packet; GRE and VXLAN only encapsulate.
Each wrapper costs 50 to 80 bytes of MTU, so lower the inner MTU or clamp the MSS.
Plan non-overlapping address ranges before joining networks.

interactive.title: Full tunnel or split?
interactive.prompt: A 600-person company moves its internal apps to a cloud network and gives staff a VPN. Most traffic during the day is video calls on a public service. Security wants internal apps reachable only over the VPN. What setup fits?

choices.label: A full tunnel for everyone
choices.feedback: This works for security but sends every video call through the company gateway, adding latency and cost for traffic that never needed the VPN.

choices.label: A split tunnel with company prefixes and internal DNS through the VPN
choices.feedback: Right: internal apps stay private behind the tunnel, internal names still resolve, and video calls go directly to the public service.

choices.label: No VPN; expose internal apps on public addresses with a firewall
choices.feedback: This breaks the requirement that internal apps are reachable only over the VPN, and puts them in front of internet scanning.

choices.label: A VXLAN overlay from every laptop
choices.feedback: VXLAN builds overlay networks between hosts and does not encrypt, so it is neither a remote-access VPN nor private over the internet.

interactive.reveal: Split tunnelling keeps the VPN for what needs it. The detail people forget is DNS: internal names must still go to the internal resolver over the tunnel, or apps fail to resolve even though routes are correct.

seeAlso.why: Encapsulation and MTU, which every tunnel header eats into
Cloud networks that site-to-site VPNs connect to
Routing and NAT, which decide what enters the tunnel and how it crosses home routers

title: Switches, VLANs and Broadcast Domains
objectives: Explain what a broadcast domain is and why its size matters
Explain how 802.1Q tags split one switch into several networks
Decide when traffic between VLANs needs a router and why loops are dangerous

cards.title: One switch, several networks
cards.body: A switch forwards frames by hardware address, and a broadcast, such as an ARP request, goes out of every port. Everything a broadcast reaches is one broadcast domain, which usually matches one IP subnet. A VLAN (virtual LAN) splits a switch into separate broadcast domains: ports in VLAN 10 never see frames from VLAN 20, as if they were on different switches. To get from one VLAN to another, traffic has to be routed.

cards.title: How a tagged frame crosses a trunk
cards.body: Access ports belong to one VLAN; trunk ports carry many and label each frame.
steps: A printer on an access port in VLAN 20 sends an ordinary, untagged frame
The switch notes that the port belongs to VLAN 20
To reach a second switch it sends the frame on a trunk port with a 4-byte 802.1Q tag holding VLAN ID 20
The second switch reads the tag and forwards the frame only to ports in VLAN 20
It strips the tag before sending it out of an access port, so the end host never sees it

cards.title: Worked example: splitting a flat office network
cards.body: Broadcasts reach every host in a domain, so their cost grows with its size.
steps: Assume 1,200 devices on one flat network, each sending 1 broadcast a second on average (ARP, discovery protocols; illustrative)
Every device receives every broadcast: 1,200 frames a second, each woken by traffic meant for someone else
Split into 6 VLANs of 200 devices, one per floor or role
Each device now receives about 200 broadcasts a second, a sixth of before
Separately, a broadcast loop or a misbehaving device now disturbs 200 devices instead of 1,200
cards.note: Result. Splitting by VLAN cuts each host’s broadcast load and the blast radius of a fault by the same factor, at the cost of a router hop between groups that need to talk.

cards.title: Routing between VLANs
cards.body: Each VLAN gets its own subnet and gateway. A layer 3 switch or a router owns a gateway address in each VLAN and routes between them, which is also the natural place for access rules: guests may reach the internet but not the accounts VLAN. A common mistake is to put two VLANs on the same subnet: hosts then try to reach each other directly with ARP, which cannot cross the VLAN boundary, so they fail without any error.

cards.title: Trap: a loop in a switched network
cards.body: Ethernet frames have no hop limit, unlike IP packets with their TTL. If two switch ports are connected in a loop, a single broadcast circles forever and multiplies at every switch, a broadcast storm that can saturate links within seconds. The Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) prevents this by blocking redundant links until they are needed. Keep it on, and take care when someone plugs a small unmanaged switch into two wall ports.

cards.title: Misconception: VLANs are a security boundary on their own
cards.body: VLANs separate traffic, but they rely on switch configuration being right. A trunk port accidentally left on a desk, or a host allowed to send tagged frames, can reach other VLANs. Treat VLANs as segmentation that makes rules possible, then enforce access with routing rules or firewalls between them, and set unused ports to an unused VLAN.

questions.prompt: An ARP request goes out from a laptop in VLAN 10. Which devices receive it?

choices.label: Every device on the switch
Only the default gateway
Every device in VLAN 10
Devices in VLAN 10 and the router’s other VLANs

questions.explanation: A broadcast stays inside its VLAN, which is its broadcast domain. Other VLANs on the same switch do not see it; the gateway is one recipient among many; and routers do not forward broadcasts between VLANs.

questions.prompt: What does a switch add to a frame it sends on a trunk port?

choices.label: A new IP header with the VLAN as the destination
A 4-byte tag holding the VLAN ID
The MAC address of the next switch
A checksum covering the VLAN membership

questions.explanation: An 802.1Q tag inserts the VLAN ID into the Ethernet header. No IP header is added, since this is layer 2; the destination MAC stays the end host’s; and the frame’s existing checksum is recalculated rather than a new one added.

questions.prompt: A laptop in VLAN 10 must reach a file server in VLAN 20. What has to exist?

choices.label: A trunk link that carries both VLANs to the server’s switch
The same IP subnet in both VLANs
A larger broadcast domain covering both
A router or layer 3 switch with a gateway in each VLAN

questions.explanation: Traffic between VLANs is routed. A trunk carries both VLANs between switches but keeps them apart rather than joining them; one subnet across two VLANs breaks ARP; and merging the domains removes the separation rather than routing across it.

questions.prompt: Someone connects two wall ports with a spare cable and the office network collapses within seconds. What happened?

choices.label: A broadcast storm from a layer 2 loop
Two DHCP servers giving out the same addresses
An IP routing loop until TTLs expired
The switch ran out of ports for new hosts

questions.explanation: Ethernet frames have no hop limit, so a broadcast circles and multiplies around the loop. Duplicate DHCP servers cause address conflicts, not a collapse in seconds; IP loops end when the TTL runs out; and a full switch refuses new links rather than flooding.

questions.prompt: Why split a 1,200-device office network into several VLANs?

choices.label: To raise the speed each switch port can carry
To let devices on the same floor skip ARP lookups
To cut broadcast load and the reach of faults
To give each device its own public address

questions.explanation: Smaller broadcast domains mean fewer broadcasts per host and a smaller blast radius, plus a place to enforce rules. Port speed is unchanged; ARP is still needed within each VLAN; and VLANs have nothing to do with public addressing.

questions.prompt: Order the journey of a frame from an access port, over a trunk, to a host on another switch.

items.label: The second switch reads the tag and picks ports in that VLAN
The switch assigns it to the port’s VLAN
The tag is removed and the frame leaves an access port
The host sends an untagged frame on an access port
The switch adds an 802.1Q tag and sends it on the trunk

questions.explanation: Tags exist only on trunks; end hosts send and receive ordinary frames.

questions.prompt: An 802.1Q VLAN ID has 12 bits, and the values 0 and 4095 are reserved. How many VLAN IDs can be used?
assumptions: Both reserved values excluded
questions.explanation: Sanity check: about four thousand is plenty for one campus but far too few for a cloud with millions of tenant networks, which is why clouds use 24-bit overlay IDs.

flashcards.back: Everything one broadcast frame reaches; usually one VLAN and one subnet.
A port that carries many VLANs, each frame tagged with its 12-bit VLAN ID.
Ethernet has no hop limit, so it blocks redundant links to stop broadcast storms.

sources.title: RFC 7348: VXLAN, section 3 on the limits of VLANs
man7: ip-link(8), VLAN type
RFC 826: An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol

mechanism.title: How a switch keeps networks apart
steps: A switch learns which hardware address lives behind which port by reading the source of each frame. Frames for a known address go out of one port; broadcasts and frames for unknown addresses are flooded out of every port in the same broadcast domain.

With VLANs configured, the switch keeps a separate address table and flood set per VLAN. An access port belongs to one VLAN, and frames arriving on it are treated as members of that VLAN, so a printer and a laptop on the same switch can be in different networks without knowing it.

When a VLAN spans several switches, the links between them are trunks. On a trunk each frame carries a 4-byte 802.1Q tag with a 12-bit VLAN ID, so the receiving switch knows which VLAN’s ports to forward it to. One VLAN on a trunk may be sent untagged, the native VLAN, which is a common source of mistakes.

Each VLAN normally has its own IP subnet and a gateway address on a router or layer 3 switch. Traffic between VLANs goes through that gateway, which can apply access rules. Hosts in different VLANs cannot reach each other by ARP, because the request never crosses into the other VLAN.

Redundant links make a network resilient but create loops, and Ethernet frames have no TTL to end them. The Spanning Tree Protocol elects a root switch and blocks enough ports to leave a loop-free tree, unblocking a backup path when an active link fails; newer designs avoid layer 2 loops by routing between switches instead.

useWhen: Separating guests, staff, phones and devices that should not see each other’s broadcasts.
Shrinking a large flat network whose broadcast load or fault reach has grown.
avoidWhen: Avoid relying on VLANs alone as an access control between sensitive groups.
Avoid stretching one VLAN across many sites; route between them instead.

rows: Routed access, small subnets per switch

numbers.title: Broadcast load before and after splitting
assumptions: 1,200 devices, 1 broadcast per device per second (illustrative)
Split into 6 equal VLANs
steps: Flat: each device receives 1,200 × 1 = 1,200 broadcasts per second.
Split: each VLAN has 1,200 ÷ 6 = 200 devices, so each receives 200 per second.
Total broadcast frames on the network drop from 1,200 × 1,200 = 1.44 million deliveries per second to 6 × 200 × 200 = 240,000.
A fault in one VLAN reaches 200 devices instead of 1,200.
numbers.result: Six VLANs cut per-host broadcast load and fault reach by six, and total broadcast deliveries by six as well.

india.title: Separating a college campus network
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: A college in Coimbatore has one flat network for 1,500 student laptops, 200 staff machines, CCTV cameras and the fee-payment counter. A student laptop running a discovery tool floods the network and the fee counter stops working during admissions week. The fix puts students, staff, cameras and the payment counter in separate VLANs, each with its own subnet. The core switch routes between them and allows the payment counter to reach only the bank gateway, while unused wall ports are put in an empty VLAN so a stray cable cannot join anything.

pitfalls.trap: “VLANs make the network secure.”
pitfalls.say: “VLANs separate broadcast domains; I’d still enforce access with rules on the router between them.”

pitfalls.trap: “Give both VLANs the same subnet so they can talk.”
pitfalls.say: “Hosts on one subnet expect ARP to work, which cannot cross VLANs; each VLAN needs its own subnet and a gateway.”

takeaways: A VLAN is a separate broadcast domain on shared switches, usually one subnet each.
Trunks carry many VLANs with a 4-byte tag holding a 12-bit ID; access ports carry one.
Traffic between VLANs must be routed, which is where access rules belong.
Ethernet has no hop limit, so loops become broadcast storms unless spanning tree blocks them.

interactive.title: Will they talk?
interactive.prompt: An engineer puts the cameras in VLAN 30 and the video recorder in VLAN 40 on the same switch, and to “keep it simple” gives both the subnet 10.5.0.0/24 with no router between them. What happens when a camera sends to the recorder?

choices.label: It works, since they are on one switch and one subnet
choices.feedback: Being on one switch does not matter: the VLANs are separate broadcast domains, so the camera’s ARP request never reaches the recorder.

choices.label: It fails silently: the ARP request stays in VLAN 30
choices.feedback: Right: the camera believes the recorder is local, sends ARP, and nothing in VLAN 30 answers, so the frames are never sent.

choices.label: It works through the default gateway
choices.feedback: The camera only uses its gateway for addresses outside its subnet, and here the recorder looks local, so the gateway is never asked.

interactive.reveal: A VLAN and a subnet should match one to one. Give VLAN 40 its own subnet and a gateway on a layer 3 switch, then allow only camera-to-recorder traffic in the rules between them.

seeAlso.why: ARP and switch learning, which VLANs divide into separate domains
Subnets, which should match VLANs one to one
Overlays, which replace VLANs when millions of networks are needed

title: DHCP and SLAAC: How a Host Gets Its Address
objectives: Trace the four DHCP messages that give a new device its address and settings
Size an address pool from lease length and how many devices come and go
Explain how IPv6 hosts form their own addresses with SLAAC

cards.title: A device with no address asks for one
cards.body: A device that joins a network has no address yet, so it cannot unicast to anyone. With DHCP (RFC 2131) it broadcasts a Discover from address 0.0.0.0 over UDP; a server answers with an Offer of an address, subnet mask, gateway and DNS servers; the device broadcasts a Request for that offer; and the server confirms with an Acknowledgement. The address is a lease: it is the device’s only for the time the server grants.

cards.title: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge
cards.body: Four messages, two from each side, often remembered as DORA.
steps: A phone joins the Wi-Fi and broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER to UDP port 67
The router, acting as a relay, forwards it as unicast to the central DHCP server, stamping its own address so the server knows which subnet to choose from
The server replies with DHCPOFFER: 10.8.4.57/22, gateway 10.8.4.1, DNS servers and a lease of 8 hours
The phone broadcasts DHCPREQUEST naming that server, which also tells any other server their offers were declined
The server commits the lease and sends DHCPACK; the phone may check by ARP that no one else uses the address

cards.title: Worked example: why a guest network ran out of addresses
cards.body: A pool must cover every device holding a lease, including ones that left hours ago.
steps: Guest Wi-Fi in a hotel lobby uses a /24: 254 usable addresses, minus the gateway, so 253 for guests
About 60 new devices join every hour; most stay 30 minutes but keep their lease until it expires (illustrative)
With 24-hour leases, addresses stay held for a day: 60 × 24 = 1,440 leases needed, far above 253
With 2-hour leases: 60 × 2 = 120 held, plus devices still present, comfortably under 253
Alternatively keep 24 hours and widen to a /21 (2,046 usable), if the address plan allows
cards.note: Result. Held leases ≈ arrivals per hour × lease hours, so short leases for transient devices or a larger pool fix exhaustion; a long lease only suits devices that stay.

cards.title: Renewing before the lease runs out
cards.body: A client does not wait until the end. At T1, by default half the lease, it asks the same server directly to extend. If that server does not answer, at T2, by default 87.5% of the lease, it broadcasts to any server. If the lease expires with no answer, it must stop using the address. This is why a DHCP outage is invisible for hours: devices keep working until their leases end, and new arrivals fail first.

cards.title: IPv6 hosts can number themselves
cards.body: On IPv6, routers send Router Advertisements announcing the network’s prefix, normally a /64. With SLAAC (RFC 4862) a host combines that prefix with a 64-bit identifier it generates itself, checks that no neighbour uses the result, and starts using it, with no server holding state. Privacy extensions (RFC 8981) add temporary addresses that change regularly, so a device is harder to track across networks. DHCPv6 (RFC 8415) still exists for networks that want a server to hand out and record addresses.

cards.title: Trap: a rogue DHCP server on the network
cards.body: Clients accept the first suitable offer, and DHCP has no built-in authentication. A home router plugged into an office port, or an attacker’s laptop, can hand out wrong gateways and DNS servers, sending traffic to the wrong place or nowhere. Managed switches offer DHCP snooping: only ports marked as trusted, towards the real servers, may send offers and acknowledgements.

questions.prompt: Why does a new device broadcast its first DHCP message instead of sending it to a server?

choices.label: Broadcasts are faster than unicast messages
DHCP servers listen only for broadcasts
It has no address and does not know the server’s
The switch requires a broadcast before learning its port

questions.explanation: Before DHCP finishes it has neither its own address nor the server’s. Broadcasts are not faster; servers also receive unicast renewals; and switches learn ports from any frame, not only broadcasts.

questions.prompt: The DHCP server sits in a data centre, but phones join Wi-Fi in a branch subnet. How do their broadcasts reach it?

choices.label: The branch router relays them as unicast, noting the subnet they came from
Routers forward broadcasts to every connected network
The phones learn the server address from DNS first
The server sends offers to the branch every few seconds unasked

questions.explanation: A relay agent turns the local broadcast into a unicast and fills in its own address, which tells the server which pool to use. Routers do not forward broadcasts; phones cannot use DNS before they have an address; and servers do not push offers unasked.

questions.prompt: A device holds an 8-hour lease. When does it first try to renew, by default?

choices.label: After 1 hour
After 4 hours
After 7 hours
When the 8 hours run out

questions.explanation: T1 defaults to half the lease, 4 hours, when it asks the same server. 7 hours is T2 (87.5%), when it broadcasts to any server; 1 hour is not a protocol timer; and waiting for expiry would leave it without an address.

questions.prompt: A café’s guest network keeps running out of addresses at lunchtime though only 40 people are inside. What is the likely fix?

choices.label: Shorter leases, so departed devices free addresses sooner
A second DHCP server handing out the same pool
Longer leases, so devices renew less often
Turning off the ARP check on offered addresses

questions.explanation: Leases held by people who already left fill the pool, so shorter leases free them sooner. Two servers sharing one pool can hand out duplicates; longer leases make exhaustion worse; and ARP checks only catch conflicts.

questions.prompt: How does an IPv6 host using SLAAC get its address?

choices.label: A DHCPv6 server assigns one from a pool
The router assigns one in its advertisement
It uses its MAC address as the full address
It combines the advertised prefix with an identifier it makes

questions.explanation: The router announces the /64 prefix and the host builds the last 64 bits itself, then checks for duplicates. DHCPv6 is a separate, stateful option; the router announces a prefix, not a host address; and a MAC address is 48 bits, not a full 128-bit address (modern hosts avoid embedding it for privacy).

questions.prompt: Order the messages when a laptop first gets an address by DHCP.

items.label: A server sends an Offer
The server sends an Acknowledgement
The laptop broadcasts a Discover
The laptop starts using the address until T1
The laptop broadcasts a Request naming that server

questions.explanation: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge; the Request is broadcast so other servers know their offers were declined.

questions.prompt: About 45 new devices join a network each hour and each keeps its lease for its full 12 hours. How many leases are held at once?
assumptions: Steady arrivals
Every device keeps its lease until expiry
questions.explanation: Design implication: a /24 with 253 usable addresses would run out; halve the lease to 6 hours (270 held) and it is still too small, so either shorten to about 4 hours or use a /22.

flashcards.back: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge: the four DHCP messages that grant a lease.
Renew with the same server at 50% of the lease; broadcast to any server at 87.5%.
An IPv6 host forms its own address from the advertised /64 prefix, with no server state.

sources.title: RFC 2131: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
RFC 4862: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration
RFC 8981: Temporary Address Extensions for Stateless Address Autoconfiguration in IPv6
RFC 8415: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)

mechanism.title: How a host goes from no address to a working one
steps: A host joining an IPv4 network starts with no address. It sends DHCPDISCOVER from 0.0.0.0 to the broadcast address on UDP port 67, with a random transaction ID so it can match replies, and its hardware address so a server can reach it.

Each server that can serve the subnet sends DHCPOFFER with an address and options: mask, default gateway, DNS servers, lease time. If the server sits on another subnet, a relay agent on the local router forwards the broadcast as unicast and records its own address in the message, which the server uses to choose a pool for that subnet.

The host picks one offer and broadcasts DHCPREQUEST naming the chosen server. The chosen server records the lease and replies with DHCPACK; the others treat the request as a polite no. The host may send an ARP probe for the address and, if someone answers, declines it and starts over.

The lease starts a clock. At T1, by default half the lease, the host unicasts a renewal to its server; at T2, by default seven-eighths of the lease, it broadcasts to any server; at expiry it must stop using the address. When the host leaves, it may send DHCPRELEASE, but phones that walk out of range usually do not, so their leases simply run out.

IPv6 networks usually work differently. Routers multicast Router Advertisements with the prefix and flags. With SLAAC, the host appends its own 64-bit interface identifier, runs duplicate address detection with its neighbours, and starts using the address; privacy extensions add short-lived temporary addresses. Flags in the advertisement can tell hosts to use DHCPv6 instead, or as well, for addresses or for options such as DNS servers.

useWhen: Any network where devices join and leave without manual configuration.
Giving each subnet the right gateway and DNS servers from one central place.
avoidWhen: Avoid DHCP for core infrastructure such as routers and DNS servers themselves; give them static addresses.
Avoid long leases on networks full of short visits.

rows: IPv6 networks that must record who had which address

numbers.title: Sizing a guest pool from arrivals and lease time
assumptions: A railway waiting hall: about 400 new devices per hour at peak (illustrative)
Lease length L hours; visits mostly under an hour
steps: Held leases ≈ arrivals per hour × L.
With L = 24: 400 × 24 = 9,600 leases, which needs a /18 (16,382 usable) or larger.
With L = 1: 400 × 1 = 400 leases, plus margin for bursts: a /22 (1,022 usable) has room.
Renewals at T1 = 30 minutes: devices still present renew about 2 times an hour, a small load for a DHCP server.
numbers.result: Cutting the lease from a day to an hour shrinks the pool needed from about 9,600 addresses to about 400 under these assumptions.

india.title: Wi-Fi at a busy railway station
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: A station Wi-Fi in a city such as Lucknow sees hundreds of phones arrive and leave every hour, most staying under an hour. If the network hands out day-long leases, its pool fills by mid-morning and new arrivals connect to Wi-Fi but get no address, which users see as “connected, no internet”. Short leases keep the number of held addresses close to the number of phones actually present, and DHCP snooping on the access switches stops a passenger’s portable router from handing out its own addresses.

pitfalls.trap: “The DHCP server is down but everything still works, so it is fine.”
pitfalls.say: “Existing devices keep their leases until T1 and T2 fail; new arrivals break first and the rest follow as leases expire.”

pitfalls.trap: “Make leases longer to reduce load.”
pitfalls.say: “Renewals are cheap; long leases on a busy guest network exhaust the pool. I’d size the pool from arrivals × lease time.”

takeaways: DHCP grants a lease in four messages: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.
Relay agents carry broadcasts to a central server and tell it which subnet to serve.
Held leases ≈ arrivals per hour × lease hours; size pools and leases together.
IPv6 hosts usually form their own addresses with SLAAC from the router’s /64 prefix.

interactive.title: Size the guest pool
interactive.prompt: About 60 devices join a guest network each hour and keep 8-hour leases, so about 480 leases are held at once. Slide the prefix length and find the smallest subnet that fits.
interactive.takeaway: A /24 holds 254 hosts and runs out; a /23 holds 510, just enough with little margin. Shortening the lease to 2 hours would bring the need down to about 120 and let the /24 work.

seeAlso.why: IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, which DHCP and SLAAC hand out
ARP, which DHCP clients use to check that an offered address is free
Subnet sizing, which sets how many leases a pool can hold

title: Data-Centre Fabrics: Leaf-Spine and Oversubscription
objectives: Explain why data centres wire every leaf switch to every spine
Calculate an oversubscription ratio and what it means for traffic between racks
Predict how a fabric degrades when a spine fails or two large flows collide

cards.title: From trees to a fabric
cards.body: Older data centres used a tree: racks connected to aggregation switches, which connected to a core, so traffic between distant racks squeezed through a few big boxes. Modern ones use a leaf-spine (Clos) fabric. Each rack has a leaf switch, and every leaf connects to every spine. Any two servers in different racks are then exactly three switch hops apart (leaf, spine, leaf), and the many spines give many equal paths that equal-cost multipath (ECMP) spreads flows across.

cards.title: A packet from rack 3 to rack 17
cards.body: Every path between two leaves goes up to one spine and down again.
steps: A server in rack 3 sends to a server in rack 17
Leaf 3 has four uplinks, one to each spine, and all four are equal-cost routes to rack 17’s prefix
It hashes the flow’s five-tuple and picks spine 2 for this flow
Spine 2 has one link to every leaf and sends the packet down to leaf 17
Another flow between the same racks may hash to spine 4; each flow stays on its own path

cards.title: Worked example: the oversubscription ratio of a rack
cards.body: Compare what servers can send with what the leaf can carry upwards.
steps: A leaf has 48 server ports at 25 Gbit/s: 48 × 25 = 1,200 Gbit/s towards servers
It has 6 uplinks at 100 Gbit/s: 6 × 100 = 600 Gbit/s towards the spines
Oversubscription = 1,200 ÷ 600 = 2:1
If every server in the rack sends off-rack at once, each gets about 25 ÷ 2 = 12.5 Gbit/s
Traffic that stays inside the rack is not limited by the uplinks at all
cards.note: Result. A 2:1 rack gives each server half its port speed when everyone talks to other racks at once. Fabrics for storage or training clusters aim for 1:1; web tiers often accept 3:1 because their servers rarely saturate together.

cards.title: Losing a spine costs a share, not the whole path
cards.body: With four spines, each carries about a quarter of leaf-to-leaf traffic. When one fails, routing withdraws it, ECMP rehashes onto the remaining three and capacity between racks falls by 25%, which a fabric sized with headroom absorbs. Flows that were on the failed spine reset or retransmit; the rest carry on. Adding a spine adds capacity the same way, which is why fabrics grow by adding spines and leaves rather than buying a bigger core.

cards.title: Trap: assuming ECMP balances bytes
cards.body: ECMP balances flows, not bytes. Two long, heavy flows, such as backups or replica rebuilds, can hash to the same uplink while other uplinks sit idle, so that link saturates and everything sharing it sees loss and latency. Averages of link utilisation hide this. Watch per-link peaks, split very large transfers across several connections, and give bulk traffic its own schedule or class.

cards.title: Routing all the way down
cards.body: Large fabrics avoid stretching layer 2 between racks: each leaf routes its rack’s subnet, and leaves and spines exchange routes with BGP, as RFC 7938 describes. A failure then becomes a routing change, with no spanning tree blocking half the links and no broadcast storm able to cross racks. Virtual networks for tenants or containers ride on top as overlays.

questions.prompt: In a leaf-spine fabric, how many switch hops separate servers in two different racks?

choices.label: It depends on how far apart the racks sit
Three: leaf, spine, leaf
One: the shared spine
Five: leaf, aggregation, core, aggregation, leaf

questions.explanation: Every leaf connects to every spine, so any rack-to-rack path is up to one spine and down. Physical distance does not change the hop count; the servers connect to leaves, not spines; and five hops describes the older three-tier tree.

questions.prompt: A leaf has 32 server ports at 10 Gbit/s and 4 uplinks at 40 Gbit/s. What is its oversubscription ratio?
questions.explanation: Down: 32 × 10 = 320 Gbit/s; up: 4 × 40 = 160 Gbit/s; 320 ÷ 160 = 2:1. 1:1 would need 320 Gbit/s of uplinks; 4:1 and 8:1 compare port counts or one uplink rather than total capacity.

questions.prompt: A fabric has four spines, and one fails. What happens to capacity between racks?

choices.label: It falls by about a quarter
It halves until the spine returns
It is unchanged, since spines are standbys
Racks lose contact until spanning tree reconverges

questions.explanation: Each spine carried about a quarter of the paths, and ECMP shifts flows to the other three. Halving would mean losing two spines; spines are all active, not standbys; and a routed fabric does not depend on spanning tree.

questions.prompt: Average uplink use is 40%, yet one uplink shows drops during nightly backups. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The uplink has a faulty optic
The oversubscription ratio is below 1:1
Two heavy backup flows hashed onto the same uplink
The spine is forwarding traffic by MAC address

questions.explanation: ECMP places whole flows, so large flows can collide on one link while averages look fine. A faulty optic drops at all hours, not only at backup time; a ratio below 1:1 means more uplink than downlink; and spines in a routed fabric forward by IP.

questions.prompt: Which workload most needs a 1:1 fabric rather than 3:1?

choices.label: Web servers that mostly answer users
Servers that mostly talk within their own rack
A tier of caches serving small objects
A training cluster exchanging data between racks

questions.explanation: Distributed training and storage rebuilds send heavy traffic between racks at the same time, exactly what oversubscription limits. Web and cache tiers rarely saturate together; and traffic within a rack never reaches the uplinks.

questions.prompt: Order how a leaf forwards a new flow to another rack.

items.label: It hashes the five-tuple to pick one uplink
The leaf looks up the destination rack’s prefix
Later packets of the flow follow the same spine
It finds one equal-cost route per spine
The chosen spine forwards down to the destination leaf

questions.explanation: Lookup, equal-cost choices, a per-flow hash, then the same path for the rest of the flow.

questions.prompt: A leaf serves 48 servers at 25 Gbit/s and has 8 uplinks at 100 Gbit/s. What is the oversubscription ratio, as down ÷ up?
assumptions: All ports run at line rate
Traffic leaves the rack
questions.explanation: Design implication: at 1.5:1 every server still gets about 16.7 Gbit/s off-rack when all send at once; reaching 1:1 needs 12 uplinks.

flashcards.back: Every rack switch (leaf) links to every spine, so rack-to-rack is always leaf, spine, leaf.
Server-facing capacity ÷ uplink capacity; 2:1 halves each server’s share when all send off-rack.
It balances flows, not bytes, so two elephant flows can collide on one link.

sources.title: RFC 7938: Use of BGP for Routing in Large-Scale Data Centers
RFC 2992: Analysis of an Equal-Cost Multi-Path Algorithm
Al-Fares et al.: A Scalable, Commodity Data Center Network Architecture (SIGCOMM 2008)
Singh et al.: Jupiter Rising (SIGCOMM 2015)

mechanism.title: How a Clos fabric spreads traffic between racks
steps: Each rack’s servers plug into a leaf switch, sometimes called top of rack. The leaf owns the rack’s subnet and is its servers’ default gateway, so traffic leaving the rack is routed from the first hop.

Every leaf has one uplink to every spine, and spines connect only to leaves. Two servers in different racks are therefore always leaf, spine, leaf apart, and the fabric offers as many equal paths between any two racks as it has spines.

Leaves and spines run a routing protocol, often BGP as in RFC 7938, so each leaf learns every other rack’s prefix through every spine. Equal-cost multipath hashes each flow’s addresses and ports to choose an uplink, keeping each flow on one path so its packets stay in order.

Capacity between racks is set by the uplinks. The oversubscription ratio, server-facing capacity divided by uplink capacity, says how much each server gets when everyone in the rack sends off-rack at once; 1:1 means full port speed, 3:1 a third.

Failures and growth are both arithmetic. A failed spine removes its share of paths and routing moves its flows to the rest; adding a spine adds a share. The number of leaves is limited by spine port count, and very large fabrics add a further layer of spines on the same principle.

useWhen: Building or reasoning about a data-centre network with heavy traffic between racks.
Sizing uplinks for storage, analytics or training clusters.
avoidWhen: Avoid stretching one layer 2 network across racks in a fabric.
Avoid reading average link use as proof there is no congestion.

rows: A core failure halves or cuts capacity

numbers.title: Sizing a rack for a storage cluster
assumptions: 40 storage servers per rack at 25 Gbit/s (illustrative)
Rebuild traffic can run every server near line rate off-rack
Uplinks at 100 Gbit/s
steps: Server-facing capacity: 40 × 25 = 1,000 Gbit/s.
For 1:1, uplinks must carry 1,000 Gbit/s: 1,000 ÷ 100 = 10 uplinks, so 10 spines.
With 5 uplinks the ratio is 1,000 ÷ 500 = 2:1, and each server gets 12.5 Gbit/s during a rebuild.
With 10 spines, one spine failure cuts rack capacity by 10%, to 900 Gbit/s, or 0.9 of line rate per server.
numbers.result: A storage rack needs ten 100 Gbit/s uplinks for 1:1; with five, rebuilds run at half speed.

india.title: Planning a data hall for a payments platform
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: A payments company in Bengaluru builds a new data hall with 30 racks. Its API servers rarely saturate their links, so their racks use 3:1 leaves and save on spine ports. The ledger database and its replicas copy data between racks constantly and rebuild whole nodes after failures, so their racks get 1:1 uplinks. With six spines, losing one costs about 17% of rack-to-rack capacity, which the team checks fits inside the headroom they keep before festival-season peaks.

pitfalls.trap: “The network is only 40% used, so it is not the bottleneck.”
pitfalls.say: “Averages hide flow collisions; I’d look at per-link peaks during the slow period.”

pitfalls.trap: “Buy a bigger core switch to add capacity.”
pitfalls.say: “In a leaf-spine fabric I’d add spines; each one adds an equal share of paths.”

takeaways: Leaf-spine links every leaf to every spine, so racks are always three hops apart.
Oversubscription = server-facing ÷ uplink capacity; it limits traffic between racks only.
Losing one of N spines costs about 1/N of capacity between racks.
ECMP balances flows, not bytes; watch per-link peaks for colliding heavy flows.

interactive.title: One spine down
interactive.prompt: A fabric has four spines and runs at 70% of rack-to-rack capacity at peak. One spine fails during the peak. What do users see?

choices.label: Nothing at all
choices.feedback: Flows on the failed spine break and must reconnect, and the remaining spines now carry more than they were sized for at this load.

choices.label: Congestion: the remaining spines would need about 93% each
choices.feedback: Right: 70% of four spines’ capacity moved onto three is 70 × 4 ÷ 3 ≈ 93%, close to full, so queues and loss rise.

choices.label: A full outage between racks
choices.feedback: Three spines still connect every leaf to every other, so traffic keeps flowing, just with less headroom.

choices.label: Traffic halves to match capacity
choices.feedback: Capacity falls by a quarter, not a half, and senders do not halve their demand on their own.

interactive.reveal: Plan peak use so that the fabric minus one spine still fits: with four spines, keep peak below about 75% of total capacity, since 75 × 4 ÷ 3 = 100%.

seeAlso.why: ECMP and routing, which choose the spine for each flow
VLANs and broadcast domains, which fabrics keep inside a rack
Loss and throughput, which suffer when flows collide on one link

title: DNS Security and Privacy: DNSSEC, DoT and DoH
objectives: Explain how an attacker can forge DNS answers and what makes it hard
Distinguish what DNSSEC protects from what DoT and DoH protect
Anticipate the outages and blind spots each one can cause

cards.title: Plain DNS trusts whatever arrives first
cards.body: Classic DNS travels over UDP port 53 without encryption or signatures. A resolver accepts the first reply whose question, transaction ID and port match its query. An attacker who can see the query can answer it; one who cannot see it must guess the 16-bit ID and the source port before the real answer arrives. A forged answer accepted by a resolver is cached for its TTL and served to everyone behind it: cache poisoning.

cards.title: How a DNSSEC answer is checked
cards.body: Each zone signs its records, and its parent vouches for its key.
steps: A validating resolver asks for the A record of shop.example and gets it with an RRSIG signature
It fetches example’s DNSKEY and checks the signature with it
It checks that key against the DS record the .example parent zone published, signed by the parent
It repeats up to the root, whose key the resolver already trusts
If every link verifies, the answer is authentic; if any fails, the resolver returns SERVFAIL

cards.title: Worked example: why random source ports matter
cards.body: An off-path attacker must match both the transaction ID and the source port.
steps: With only a 16-bit ID, a forged reply has a 1 in 65,536 chance
Flooding 1,000 forged replies per query attempt gives about 1,000 ÷ 65,536 ≈ 1.5% per try
Randomising the source port over Linux’s default range adds 28,232 choices (32,768 to 60,999)
Combined: 65,536 × 28,232 ≈ 1.85 billion combinations
The same 1,000 forgeries now succeed about 1,000 ÷ 1.85 billion ≈ 0.00005% per try
cards.note: Result. Port randomisation (RFC 5452) makes blind forging tens of thousands of times harder, but it does not stop an attacker who can see the traffic; only signatures (DNSSEC) or encryption (DoT, DoH) close that gap.

cards.title: DNSSEC proves, DoT and DoH hide
cards.body: DNSSEC (RFC 4033–4035) adds signatures, so a validating resolver can prove an answer came from the zone owner unchanged. It does not encrypt anything: anyone on the path still sees the names. DNS over TLS (RFC 7858, port 853) and DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484, port 443) encrypt the hop from a device to its resolver, so the café Wi-Fi cannot read or alter queries, but the resolver itself still sees every name and must be trusted. They solve different problems and work together.

cards.title: Trap: DNSSEC failures look like the site is down
cards.body: A validating resolver that cannot verify an answer returns SERVFAIL, not the unsigned answer. Expired signatures, a key rollover that forgot to update the DS record at the parent, or a provider change that left old DS records behind take the whole domain offline for users of validating resolvers, while others see no problem. Automate signing and rollovers, monitor signature expiry, and remove the DS record before moving to a provider that does not sign.

cards.title: Edge case: encrypted DNS and internal names
cards.body: Company networks often answer internal names, such as wiki.corp.example, only from their own resolver. An application that sends DoH straight to a public resolver bypasses it, so internal names fail and company filtering is skipped. Networks can signal their own encrypted resolver, and managed devices can be configured to use it; check this before rolling out encrypted DNS on laptops.

questions.prompt: An attacker cannot see a resolver’s queries. What must a forged reply match to be accepted?

choices.label: The resolver’s TLS certificate
The question, the 16-bit ID and the source port
Only the name being queried
The authoritative server’s hardware address

questions.explanation: Plain DNS accepts the first reply that matches the question, ID and port. Plain DNS has no TLS; matching the name alone was never enough; and hardware addresses do not survive across routers.

questions.prompt: What does DNSSEC give a validating resolver?

choices.label: Proof the answer came unchanged from the zone owner
Encryption of the query so the network cannot read it
A faster lookup through cached signatures
A guarantee the website itself is safe to use

questions.explanation: DNSSEC is about authenticity and integrity. It encrypts nothing, so names stay visible; validation adds work rather than speed; and a correct address says nothing about whether the site is trustworthy.

questions.prompt: A laptop on café Wi-Fi switches to DNS over HTTPS with a public resolver. Who can still see which names it looks up?

choices.label: The café’s Wi-Fi operator
Nobody at all
The public resolver it now uses
Every authoritative server on the way, for every name

questions.explanation: Encryption hides queries from the network between the laptop and the resolver, but the resolver decrypts them to answer. The café sees only HTTPS to the resolver; and authoritative servers see the resolver’s queries for their own zones, not every name.

questions.prompt: Users of some ISPs cannot reach a domain, while others can. The team recently moved DNS providers. What should they check first?

choices.label: Whether the new provider supports IPv6
Whether the TTLs are too long
Whether the web server’s TLS certificate expired
Whether the parent still holds the old provider’s DS record

questions.explanation: A stale DS record makes validating resolvers reject the new, differently signed zone with SERVFAIL, while non-validating resolvers work. IPv6 and TTLs would not split users by resolver like this; and an expired TLS certificate fails for everyone, after the lookup.

questions.prompt: After a browser enables DNS over HTTPS to a public resolver, staff cannot open internal sites by name. Why?

choices.label: DoH cannot carry internal names
The public resolver cannot see the company’s internal zone
Internal sites need DNSSEC to be found over DoH
HTTPS on port 443 is blocked inside the office

questions.explanation: Internal names exist only on the company resolver, which the browser now bypasses. DoH carries any name; DNSSEC is not required to resolve names; and if port 443 were blocked, ordinary websites would fail too.

questions.prompt: Order how a validating resolver checks a signed answer.

items.label: Check that key against the parent’s DS record
Accept the answer, or return SERVFAIL on any failure
Receive the record with its RRSIG signature
Repeat up the chain to the root
Check the signature with the zone’s DNSKEY

questions.explanation: Each zone’s key is vouched for by its parent, up to the root key the resolver already trusts.

questions.prompt: To forge a DNS reply blind, an attacker must match a random transaction ID (65,536 values) and a random source port (28,232 values). Roughly how many billion forged packets would cover every pair?
assumptions: Both values uniformly random
The attacker cannot see queries
questions.explanation: Sanity check: that is about 28,000 times harder than guessing the ID alone, but an attacker on the path sees both values and needs no guessing.

flashcards.back: A forged answer accepted by a resolver and served to everyone behind it until the TTL ends.
DNSSEC signs answers (authentic, not private); DoT and DoH encrypt the device-to-resolver hop.
SERVFAIL only from validating resolvers, often after a key or provider change.

sources.title: RFC 4033: DNS Security Introduction and Requirements
RFC 5452: Measures for Making DNS More Resilient against Forged Answers
RFC 7858: DNS over Transport Layer Security (TLS)
RFC 8484: DNS Queries over HTTPS (DoH)

mechanism.title: Where DNS can be attacked and what each defence covers
steps: A device’s stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, which asks root, top-level and authoritative servers. Classic DNS sends each of these as unencrypted, unsigned UDP, so there are two places to attack: the hop from the device to its resolver, and the hops from the resolver to authoritative servers.

An attacker on the network path, such as a hostile Wi-Fi hotspot, can read queries and answer them first. An attacker off the path must guess the transaction ID and source port; RFC 5452’s randomisation makes that a guess among billions, but a successful forgery is cached for its TTL and served to every user of that resolver.

DNSSEC lets the zone owner sign each set of records. The resolver checks the signature with the zone’s key, the key against a DS record signed by the parent, and so on to the root key. A forged or altered answer fails the check, and the resolver returns SERVFAIL rather than a lie, so DNSSEC protects every hop, but only for signed zones and validating resolvers.

DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS wrap the device-to-resolver hop in TLS. The local network can no longer read or change queries, and DoH looks like any other HTTPS traffic on port 443. The resolver still sees every query, so the choice of resolver becomes a privacy decision, and internal names only work if the encrypted resolver is the company’s own.

Each defence has an operational cost. DNSSEC needs keys rolled and signatures refreshed, or the zone goes dark for validating users. Encrypted DNS moves queries away from network operators’ resolvers, which can break internal names and filtering unless devices are pointed at the right resolver.

useWhen: Signing a zone whose answers attackers would profit from changing, such as a bank or payment domain.
Encrypting DNS for devices that use untrusted networks such as public Wi-Fi.
avoidWhen: Avoid enabling DNSSEC without automated signing and monitoring of expiry.
Avoid sending managed laptops’ DNS to a public resolver when internal names matter.

rows: Forged or altered answers on any hop
Reading or altering the device-to-resolver hop
The resolver itself, and unsigned answers it fetches

numbers.title: How long a poisoned answer lasts
assumptions: A forged A record is accepted with a TTL of 86,400 s (the attacker chooses it; illustrative)
