The resolver serves 50,000 users who visit the site about twice a day (illustrative)
steps: The forged answer stays cached for up to 86,400 s, a whole day.
Lookups served from cache in that day: 50,000 × 2 = 100,000.
Every one of them goes to the attacker’s address unless the resolver’s cache is flushed.
With DNSSEC validation, the forged record fails its signature check and is never cached.
numbers.result: One accepted forgery can misdirect a resolver’s whole user base for as long as the attacker’s TTL; validation stops it at the door.

india.title: Government domains and DNSSEC in India
india.label: Public example
india.body: Public DNSSEC checking tools such as DNSViz let anyone inspect whether a domain, for example a government or bank domain under .in or .gov.in, publishes signed records and a DS record at its parent. A user on a validating resolver who looks up a signed domain gets SERVFAIL rather than an altered answer if the signatures fail. Teams running such domains in India, as anywhere, need automated signing and expiry monitoring, because a missed rollover makes the domain unreachable only for users of validating resolvers, which makes the outage look partial and confusing.

pitfalls.trap: “We use DoH, so our DNS is authenticated.”
pitfalls.say: “DoH encrypts the hop to the resolver; whether answers are authentic depends on DNSSEC and on trusting that resolver.”

pitfalls.trap: “Some users can’t reach us; it must be their ISP.”
pitfalls.say: “If only validating resolvers fail, I’d check our DNSSEC chain first: DS records, key rollover and signature expiry.”

takeaways: Plain DNS accepts the first matching reply; random IDs and ports make blind forgery hard, not impossible.
DNSSEC signs answers so resolvers can reject forgeries; it encrypts nothing.
DoT and DoH encrypt the device-to-resolver hop; the resolver still sees every name.
Broken DNSSEC chains show up as SERVFAIL for validating resolvers only.

interactive.title: Who can reach the domain?
interactive.prompt: A company moves its domain to a new DNS provider that does not sign zones, but forgets to remove the DS record the old, signing provider had published at the parent. What happens next?

choices.label: Nothing changes for anyone
choices.feedback: Validating resolvers still find the DS record, expect signatures, and reject the new unsigned answers.

choices.label: Users of validating resolvers get SERVFAIL; others are fine
choices.feedback: Right: the parent says the zone is signed, the new answers have no valid signatures, so validators refuse them, while non-validating resolvers never check.

choices.label: Every user gets the old provider’s addresses
choices.feedback: Once caches expire, resolvers ask the new provider; the problem is that validators reject its answers, not that old ones persist.

choices.label: Browsers show a certificate warning
choices.feedback: Certificates are checked after the lookup; here the lookup itself fails for validating users, so the browser never reaches the site.

interactive.reveal: DNSSEC failures are partial outages: only users behind validating resolvers break. Remove or update the DS record at the parent before switching to a provider that signs differently or not at all, and wait out its TTL.

title: Mobile and Wi-Fi Networks: The Last Mile
objectives: Explain why wireless links add jitter and loss that wired links do not
Account for radio wake-up time and battery cost when designing mobile traffic
Keep sessions alive across network changes and short NAT timeouts

cards.title: Air is a shared, noisy medium
cards.body: On Wi-Fi, every device on a channel takes turns: a sender listens, waits a random back-off if the air is busy, and transmits only when it is clear. Frames that are corrupted by interference are retried by the radio itself, invisibly to TCP, so loss often shows up as extra delay instead. Signal strength sets the data rate, so a phone at the edge of coverage both sends slowly and takes airtime from everyone else. Wireless latency therefore varies far more than a cable’s.

cards.title: What happens when an idle phone sends a request
cards.body: On cellular networks, the radio has to wake before data can move.
steps: The phone has been idle, so its radio is in a low-power state with no channel to the network
The app sends a request; the radio first negotiates a connection with the cell tower
Only then do the DNS lookup, TCP and TLS handshakes and the request itself go out
After the reply, the radio stays in a high-power state for several seconds in case more data comes
It then drops back to idle, and the next request pays the wake-up again

cards.title: Worked example: chatty requests on a sleepy radio
cards.body: Spreading small requests out keeps waking the radio and keeping it awake.
steps: Assume a wake-up of 100 ms, a round trip of 80 ms and a high-power tail of 5 s after each burst (illustrative figures; real values vary by network)
An app sends 6 analytics pings, one every 20 s: each pays 100 ms + 80 ms = 180 ms and keeps the radio awake 5 s
Radio awake time: 6 × 5 s = 30 s, plus six wake-ups
Batched into one request at the end: one wake-up, one round trip, one 5 s tail
Awake time falls from about 30 s to about 5 s, a sixth, for the same data
cards.note: Result. On mobile, the number of separate bursts matters more than the bytes. Batch background work, piggyback on requests the user is already waiting for, and let the platform schedule deferrable uploads.

cards.title: When the network changes under a connection
cards.body: Walking out of Wi-Fi range moves a phone to cellular and gives it a new IP address. A TCP connection is identified by its addresses and ports, so every open connection dies and must be rebuilt, including TLS. QUIC (RFC 9000) identifies connections by connection IDs instead, so a client can migrate an open connection to the new path after validating it. Either way, apps should treat a network change as normal: retry idempotent requests and resume uploads from the last confirmed byte.

cards.title: Trap: keep-alives tuned for a data centre
cards.body: Mobile operators often place many users behind carrier-grade NAT, whose idle timers can be short: RFC 4787 asks for at least 2 minutes for UDP and RFC 5382 for over 2 hours for established TCP, but some carrier devices use much shorter timers in practice. A long-lived connection with no traffic for longer than the timer silently loses its mapping, and the next message from the server is dropped. Sending a keep-alive every few seconds keeps it, but also keeps the radio awake and drains the battery. Use the platform’s push service for wake-ups, and keep-alives near, not far below, the timer.

cards.title: Misconception: more bars means a fast connection
cards.body: Signal strength is only one factor. A crowded cell or a busy Wi-Fi channel shares its capacity among everyone on it, so full bars at a stadium can still mean seconds of latency. Large buffers in the radio network can add hundreds of milliseconds under load. Measure from real devices, split latency by network type, and design for the slow tail: small first responses, compressed payloads and timeouts that allow for wireless variance.

questions.prompt: Why does Wi-Fi loss often show up as extra latency rather than as TCP retransmissions?

choices.label: TCP turns off loss detection on Wi-Fi links
The radio retries corrupted frames itself before TCP notices
Wi-Fi frames are larger than Ethernet frames
Access points queue every packet until the signal improves

questions.explanation: Link-layer retries hide most losses from TCP but take airtime, which adds delay. TCP has no special Wi-Fi mode; frame size does not explain it; and access points do not hold packets indefinitely waiting for signal.

questions.prompt: The first request after a phone sits idle is slower than the next few. What adds the extra time?

choices.label: The radio must connect to the network before sending
The phone’s CPU is in a power-saving mode
The server’s connection pool has gone cold
The cell tower has to fetch the phone’s profile first

questions.explanation: An idle radio first sets up a channel with the tower, which costs time before any packet moves. CPU wake is microseconds by comparison; a cold server pool would affect all clients, not one phone after idling; and the tower does not fetch a profile per request.

questions.prompt: An app sends a small analytics event every 15 seconds in the background. What change saves the most battery?

choices.label: Compress each event to half its size
Switch the events from TCP to UDP
Batch events and send them together less often
Send each event to a nearer server

questions.explanation: Each separate burst wakes the radio and keeps it in high power for seconds, so fewer bursts matter most. Halving tiny payloads saves little; UDP still wakes the radio; and a nearer server shortens a round trip but not the awake tail.

questions.prompt: A user walks from Wi-Fi onto cellular in the middle of a large upload over TCP. What happens?

choices.label: The upload continues on the new network unchanged
The phone keeps its Wi-Fi IP address on cellular
The upload waits until Wi-Fi returns, then resumes
The connection breaks, because its address changed

questions.explanation: TCP connections are bound to their addresses, so a new IP means a new connection; the app should resume from the last confirmed byte. Seamless continuation needs QUIC migration or a multipath transport; and phones get a new address on each network.

questions.prompt: A chat app keeps an idle connection to its server, and messages sometimes never arrive after a few minutes of silence. What is a likely cause?

choices.label: The carrier NAT dropped the idle mapping
The server ran out of file descriptors
The phone’s DNS cache expired
TCP slow start reset the window to zero

questions.explanation: An idle mapping that times out means the server’s next packets are dropped at the NAT. File-descriptor exhaustion would refuse new connections; DNS is not used on an open connection; and slow start never sets the window to zero.

questions.prompt: Order what happens when an idle phone makes a request.

items.label: The radio stays in high power for a few seconds
The radio is idle with no channel to the tower
The radio drops back to idle
DNS, handshakes and the request go out
The radio connects to the network

questions.explanation: Wake, send, linger, sleep. Every separate burst repeats the whole cycle.

questions.prompt: A radio stays awake 5 s after each burst. An app sends 12 separate bursts an hour; batched, it would send 2. How many seconds of awake tail per hour does batching save?
assumptions: Bursts far enough apart that tails do not overlap
questions.explanation: Sanity check: from 60 s to 10 s of tail per hour, a sixth, without changing how much data is sent.

flashcards.back: Shared airtime, random back-offs and link-layer retries that turn loss into delay.
After a burst the cellular radio stays in high power for seconds; fewer bursts save battery.
A new IP breaks TCP connections; QUIC can migrate with connection IDs; apps must resume.

mechanism.title: What the wireless hop does to your traffic
steps: On Wi-Fi, devices share a channel and take turns. Each sender listens before it transmits and waits a random back-off when the air is busy, and the receiver acknowledges each frame. A corrupted frame is resent by the radio, so the transport above sees a delay rather than a loss, and a weak device using a low data rate takes more airtime from everyone.

On cellular networks, the phone’s radio moves between states. In idle it saves power but has no channel; before sending it must negotiate one with the network, which takes time. After traffic ends it lingers in a high-power state for a few seconds in case more data follows, then drops back. Each separate burst therefore costs a wake-up delay and a tail of battery use.

Radio networks buffer heavily to ride out fading and scheduling, so latency under load can grow by hundreds of milliseconds, and loss-based congestion control fills those buffers. Round-trip times are both higher and more variable than on wired paths, which stretches timeouts and makes the slow tail of requests much longer than the median.

Moving between networks changes the device’s IP address. TCP connections, named by addresses and ports, break and must be rebuilt with fresh handshakes. QUIC names connections with connection IDs so a client can validate a new path and keep going; multipath transports can use both networks at once.

Mobile operators often put subscribers behind carrier-grade NAT. Idle mappings expire, after which inbound packets for that flow are dropped. Apps that need server-initiated messages either keep mappings alive with periodic traffic, at a battery cost, or rely on the platform’s push channel, which shares one connection across all apps.

useWhen: Designing APIs and sync for phone apps on cellular or public Wi-Fi.
Setting timeouts, retries and keep-alives for clients on wireless links.
avoidWhen: Avoid frequent background polling on mobile when a push channel exists.
Avoid timeouts tuned for data-centre round trips on wireless clients.

rows: Each pays wake-up and round trips

numbers.title: A screen that makes five calls in a row
assumptions: Wake-up 100 ms, round trip 80 ms on cellular (illustrative)
Five dependent API calls on one warm connection
Server time 20 ms per call
steps: Sequential calls: 100 ms wake-up + 5 × (80 + 20) ms = 600 ms.
One combined call that returns everything: 100 + 80 + 5 × 20 = 280 ms, if the server runs the five steps itself.
On Wi-Fi with a 20 ms round trip and no wake-up: 5 × 40 = 200 ms versus 20 + 100 = 120 ms.
The combined call saves 320 ms on cellular but only 80 ms on Wi-Fi.
numbers.result: Round trips cost four times more on cellular here, so collapsing dependent calls matters most where users are on mobile.

india.title: Designing for patchy mobile coverage
india.label: Illustrative example
india.body: A delivery app used by riders across Indian cities sees phones move between 4G, 5G, weak signal under flyovers and shop Wi-Fi many times a shift. Its order screen originally made five calls in a row; it is changed to one call that returns the whole screen. Location updates are batched every 30 seconds instead of sent every 5, proof-of-delivery photos upload in resumable chunks so a network change does not restart them, and new orders arrive through the platform push service rather than a polling loop.

pitfalls.trap: “The API is fast; our server time is 20 ms.”
pitfalls.say: “On cellular each round trip and radio wake-up dominate; I’d measure end-to-end latency on real devices by network type.”

pitfalls.trap: “Send a keep-alive every 10 seconds so messages always arrive.”
pitfalls.say: “That keeps the radio awake and drains the battery; I’d use the platform push channel and keep-alives near the NAT timeout.”

takeaways: Wireless links share airtime and retry frames, turning loss into jitter.
Cellular radios pay a wake-up and a high-power tail per burst; batch to save both.
A network change gives a new IP and breaks TCP; resume or use QUIC migration.
Carrier NAT drops idle mappings; prefer push channels to frequent keep-alives.

interactive.title: Which costs more battery?
interactive.prompt: Two versions of an app send the same 60 small background events an hour. Version A sends each event as it happens, roughly once a minute. Version B batches them and sends once every 15 minutes. Assume a cellular radio that stays in high power for 5 seconds after each burst. Which drains the battery more, and roughly how much awake tail does each spend per hour?

choices.label: They cost the same, since the data is identical
choices.feedback: The bytes are the same, but the number of separate bursts is not, and each burst keeps the radio awake for the tail.

choices.label: A, with about 300 s of tail against about 20 s for B
choices.feedback: Right: A has 60 bursts × 5 s = 300 s of tail; B has 4 bursts × 5 s = 20 s, about one fifteenth.

choices.label: B, because its batches are larger
choices.feedback: Larger batches take a little longer to send, but they wake the radio 4 times instead of 60, so B spends far less time awake.

interactive.reveal: On mobile, count bursts, not bytes. Batch deferrable work, send it with requests the user already triggered, and let the operating system schedule background sync.
